analogy.p: Think of the heart as a busy workshop and a coronary artery as the pipe bringing in fuel. Over time, grease sticks to the inside of the pipe (fatty deposits), so less fuel gets through and machines start to stall (chest pain, heart attack). A statin is like a filter that reduces the grease in the supply, slowing the build-up. A stent is a metal sleeve pushed inside the pipe to hold it open. A valve replacement is swapping a faulty one-way flap, and a transplant is replacing the whole workshop. The analogy breaks down because arteries are living tissue that can react, form clots and be rejected by the body, which a plumbing pipe cannot do.
analogy.t: A blocked pipe supplying a workshop

bullets: Disease: fatty material builds up, coronary arteries narrow, less blood, less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.
Statins: reduce blood cholesterol, which slows down the rate at which fatty material is deposited.
Stents: keep the coronary arteries open.
Faulty valves (do not open fully, or leak) can be replaced with biological or mechanical valves.
Heart failure: a donor heart (or heart and lungs) can be transplanted; artificial hearts keep patients alive while waiting for a transplant or let the heart rest to recover.
Command word to expect: evaluate, which needs a judgement using advantages and disadvantages.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to know that **coronary heart disease (CHD)** happens when **layers of fatty material build up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them**. This **reduces blood flow through the coronary arteries**, so the **heart muscle gets less oxygen**. You must also know four treatments: **statins**, **stents**, **replacement heart valves** (biological or mechanical) and **transplants or artificial hearts**, and you must be able to **evaluate** them. It is an 'evaluate' topic, so always think benefit, risk and cost.

bullets: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood; they are not the vena cava or aorta.
Heart muscle never rests, so it has a very high demand for oxygen and glucose.
The cavity of a blood vessel is called the **lumen**; a narrower lumen means less blood can flow.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; walls are thick, elastic and muscular.
Link: this is why the coronary arteries, not the veins, are the vessels affected by CHD.
Link: the heart is an organ in the circulatory system, studied with double circulation (see heart topics).
core.h: The coronary arteries and why the heart needs them
core.p: The heart is a muscle, and its cells need a constant supply of **oxygen and glucose** for **aerobic respiration**, which releases the energy for contraction. Blood inside the heart chambers does not feed the heart wall, so the heart has its own blood supply: the **coronary arteries**, which branch from the aorta and run over the surface of the heart. They are the vessels that become blocked in CHD. If their supply falls, the muscle cannot release enough energy and cells are damaged.

bullets: Step 1: fatty material (cholesterol) is deposited in the artery wall.
Step 2: the lumen narrows, so there is reduced blood flow through the coronary artery.
Step 3: a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle (the key AQA phrase).
Step 4: the heart muscle cannot respire aerobically fast enough, causing chest pain; if the artery blocks completely, part of the muscle can die (heart attack).
A blood clot forming on a rough, narrowed deposit can block the artery completely; this is how many heart attacks happen.
Remember: CHD is a non-communicable disease; it is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed on by contact.
core.p: In CHD, **layers of fatty material (made from cholesterol and fat) build up inside the walls of the coronary arteries**. As the deposit grows, the lumen becomes narrower, so **less blood can flow** through it. The heart muscle supplied by that artery therefore receives **less oxygen and glucose**, and aerobic respiration in its cells falls. This is the central cause-and-effect chain that mark schemes reward, and it must be written in order.

bullets: Diet high in saturated fat: raises blood cholesterol, which is deposited as fatty material.
Smoking: damages artery walls and carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried by blood.
High blood pressure: can damage artery walls, making deposits more likely.
Obesity and lack of exercise: linked to higher rates of cardiovascular disease.
Inherited factors: some people naturally have high cholesterol.
Correlation is not the same as cause: a link in data does not on its own prove the factor causes CHD (see health and risk factors).
core.h: Risk factors that make CHD more likely
core.p: CHD is a **non-communicable disease** with several **risk factors**, which are things that raise the chance of developing a disease without guaranteeing it. A diet high in saturated fat tends to raise blood cholesterol, so more fatty material can be deposited. Smoking, high blood pressure, obesity and lack of exercise are also linked to cardiovascular disease, and some people inherit a tendency to high cholesterol. Knowing the risk factors links this topic to lifestyle and to the evaluation of prevention versus treatment.

bullets: Action: reduce blood cholesterol, which slows the rate of fatty deposits in the coronary arteries.
Advantage: tablets, no surgery needed, and they can reduce the risk of heart attacks over time.
Advantage: widely used and relatively cheap compared with surgery.
Disadvantage: must be taken for a long time, so the patient must remember to take them.
Disadvantage: they can cause side effects in some people (for example muscle aches); some patients cannot take them.
Disadvantage: they slow the disease; they do not cure it or instantly unblock an artery.
Evaluation tip: statins treat the cause (cholesterol), whereas a stent treats the symptom (the narrowing).
core.p: **Statins** are drugs that **reduce the level of cholesterol in the blood**. Because there is less cholesterol available, the **rate at which fatty material is deposited in the arteries slows down**. They are taken as tablets, usually for a long time, so they are a way of managing the disease rather than a quick fix. Statins do not usually remove deposits that are already there; they slow the build-up of more.

bullets: Action: keeps the coronary artery open so that blood can flow to the heart muscle.
Advantage: quick, effective straight away, and a shorter recovery than major surgery.
Advantage: lowers the chance of the artery being blocked again in the stented section.
Disadvantage: it is an operation, so there are risks of infection, bleeding or damage to the artery.
Disadvantage: the patient may form blood clots around the stent and may need to take drugs to prevent them.
Disadvantage: it does not cure the underlying cause; the artery can narrow again or other arteries can still be affected.
Compare: stents give fast relief of narrowing; statins work slowly but treat the cause.
core.p: A **stent** is a **wire mesh tube** that is put into a narrowed coronary artery on a thin tube (a catheter) and then expanded. It **holds the artery open**, which allows blood to flow to the heart muscle again. The effect is immediate, so stents are very useful for relieving symptoms and treating emergencies such as a heart attack. However, a stent does not cure the underlying disease, and fatty material can still build up elsewhere.

bullets: Faulty valve type 1: does not open fully, so blood cannot flow forward properly.
Faulty valve type 2: leaks, so blood flows backwards through it.
Biological valves: from animals or humans; usually no need for long-term blood-thinning drugs, but they can wear out and may need replacing.
Mechanical valves: made from artificial materials; they last a long time, but the patient usually needs to take anticoagulants to stop clots forming.
Anticoagulants reduce clotting, which brings a risk of bleeding more easily.
Both are major operations, which carry risks of infection and complications.
Evaluation tip: compare lifespan of the valve with the need for lifelong medication.
core.p: Heart valves keep blood moving in one direction. A valve can become **faulty** by **not opening fully** (so blood flow is restricted) or by **developing a leak** (so blood flows backwards). A faulty valve can be replaced using either a **biological valve** (taken from a human or an animal such as a pig or cow) or a **mechanical valve** (made from artificial materials). Replacing the valve restores one-way flow, so the heart pumps blood more efficiently.

bullets: Transplant: replaces the failing heart with a healthy donor heart (or heart and lungs).
Problem: there are not enough donors, so patients wait a long time.
Problem: rejection, because the immune system attacks the donor tissue; patients take immunosuppressant drugs for life.
Immunosuppressants make the patient more likely to catch infections.
Artificial heart: a mechanical pump; no rejection by the immune system in the same way, but it is a bridge, not usually a permanent solution.
Artificial hearts can cause problems such as blood clots, infection and device failure, and the patient may need drugs to stop clotting.
Advantage of an artificial heart: it can keep the patient alive while a donor heart is found, or give the heart time to recover.
core.h: Treatment 4: heart transplants and artificial hearts
core.p: In **heart failure**, the heart can no longer pump enough blood. A **donor heart**, or a **heart and lungs**, can be **transplanted** into the patient. Transplants are major operations that need a suitable donor, and the patient's immune system may recognise the new organ as foreign. **Artificial hearts** are mechanical pumps that are occasionally used to **keep patients alive whilst they wait for a transplant**, or to **allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery**.

bullets: Compare speed: stent and transplant are quick; statins act slowly over months or years.
Compare invasiveness: statins are tablets; stents, valves and transplants are operations.
Cause versus symptom: statins slow the cause (cholesterol); stents relieve the narrowing.
Risks: infection and clots (surgery), side effects (statins), rejection (transplants).
Long term: statins and anticoagulants are taken for life; mechanical valves last but need drugs.
Always end with a conclusion that chooses a treatment for a stated situation and gives a reason.
Use data if given, e.g. percentage of patients surviving, and quote figures.
core.h: How to evaluate treatments for cardiovascular disease
core.p: 'Evaluate' means weigh up the advantages and disadvantages and reach a **justified conclusion**. A good answer for this topic compares **how quickly the treatment works**, **how invasive it is** (tablet versus surgery), whether it treats the **cause or the symptom**, the **risks and side effects**, and the **longer-term outcome and cost**. The best answers also match the treatment to the patient: a patient with early CHD may be suited to statins, whereas a patient with a badly blocked artery needs a stent.

bullets: Lower saturated fat intake to help reduce blood cholesterol.
Exercise regularly and keep to a healthy weight.
Do not smoke; limit alcohol.
Regular check-ups can find high cholesterol or blood pressure before symptoms start.
Prevention costs less than surgery for the health service and avoids operation risks.
Drawback: it relies on the person making long-term lifestyle changes.
core.p: Because treatments are expensive and carry risk, health services try to **reduce the number of people who develop CHD** in the first place. A balanced diet low in saturated fat, regular exercise, not smoking and a healthy body mass all lower the risk factors. Doctors may also give statins to people at high risk before they develop symptoms. When you evaluate, you can argue that changes to lifestyle are cheaper and have no side effects, although people find it hard to change habits.

bullets: Quote data: 'the statin group had 8% heart attacks compared with 14% in the placebo group'.
Calculate the difference, and say whether it is large or small.
A bigger sample gives more reliable results and reduces the effect of anomalies.
Look for control variables: age, sex, existing disease, other drugs.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
Write one conclusion that uses the data and mentions limits (short trial, small sample).
core.h: Interpreting data about CHD and treatments
core.p: Exam questions often give a **table or graph**, for example the percentage of patients having a heart attack with and without a statin. You should compare the **two groups**, quote **figures with units**, and calculate **percentage differences** carefully. A fair trial uses a **large sample**, patients who are alike (similar age, sex and health), and a **control group** given a placebo so that the effect of the drug can be judged. Remember that a **correlation does not prove cause**.

bullets: Circulatory system: the coronary arteries branch from the aorta to supply the heart muscle.
Respiration: less oxygen means the heart muscle cannot respire aerobically as quickly.
Immune system: antigens on a donor heart can lead to rejection.
Health and disease: risk factors and the difference between correlation and cause.
Ethical issues: shortage of donors, the cost of treatment, and allocating organs fairly.
core.p: CHD ties together several parts of the course. It links to **organisation** (the heart as an organ, the circulatory system and double circulation), to **health and disease** (non-communicable disease and risk factors), to **respiration** (the heart muscle needs oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration) and to the **immune system** (transplant rejection). It also links to **ethics and society**, because there is debate about donors, cost and who should receive scarce hearts.

bullets: A **healthy valve** opens to let blood forwards and closes to stop backflow.
A valve that **does not open fully** restricts the flow of blood.
A valve that **leaks** lets blood flow backwards, so less is pumped forwards.
A **biological valve** comes from an animal or a human donor.
A **mechanical valve** is made from artificial materials; the patient may need drugs to stop blood clotting.
Replacement needs an operation, so risks and recovery time must be weighed against the benefit.
core.h: Faulty valves: how each fault reduces circulation
core.p: Heart valves make sure blood moves in one direction through the heart. A valve can fail in two ways. If it is stiff and does not open fully, the opening is narrow so blood flow is restricted and the heart must work harder to push blood through. If it leaks, it does not close properly, so some blood flows backwards on each beat and less is pumped forward. In both cases the circulation is less efficient, so tissues may not get enough oxygen, and the valve can be replaced.

bullets: Step 1: fatty material builds up in the **coronary arteries**.
Step 2: the **lumen narrows**.
Step 3: **less blood** flows to the heart muscle.
Step 4: **less oxygen** (and glucose) is delivered.
Step 5: less **aerobic respiration**, so less energy for contraction.
Always name the coronary arteries, not just 'the arteries' or 'the heart'.
core.p: A common 4-mark question asks you to explain how CHD affects the heart. A full answer links each step to the next: layers of fatty material build up in the coronary arteries, which narrows them; this reduces blood flow through them; so less oxygen is delivered to the heart muscle; therefore the muscle cells cannot respire aerobically as quickly and release less energy for contraction. Writing the chain in order, with linking words such as 'so' and 'therefore', secures each mark.

exam: 'Describe' (2 to 3 marks): state the order of events: fatty material builds up, artery narrows, less blood flow, less oxygen to heart muscle.
'Explain how a stent helps' (2 to 3 marks): holds the artery open; so blood can flow to the heart muscle; more oxygen delivered.
'Explain how statins work' (2 marks): reduce blood cholesterol; so slow the rate of fatty material being deposited.
'Give one disadvantage' (1 mark): choose a specific one, e.g. rejection, side effects, surgery risk, must be taken for life.
Do not just say 'it is risky'. Name the risk: infection, blood clots, rejection, bleeding with anticoagulants.
'Evaluate' (4 to 6 marks): at least two treatments, advantages and disadvantages for each, then a conclusion with a reason.
A 6 mark answer uses linked ideas: because ... this means ... therefore, and ends with a clear judgement.
Use the exact phrase 'reduced blood flow' and 'lack of oxygen for the heart muscle' in disease questions.
For data questions quote figures from the table or graph with units, and calculate difference or percentage change.
Write 'lumen' or 'narrower' for the blocked space, not 'the hole gets smaller' alone.
Use 'immune system' and 'antigens' when explaining transplant rejection.
**Explain how CHD affects the heart (4 marks)**: fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them, reducing blood flow, so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

mistakes.r: The coronary ARTERIES become narrowed by fatty material.
Statins reduce blood cholesterol, which slows the rate of fatty deposits; they do not cure it.
A stent keeps the artery open; it does not remove the deposits.
mistakes.w: A stent removes the fat from the artery.

mistakes.r: The heart muscle is supplied by the coronary arteries.
mistakes.w: The heart muscle gets blood from the blood inside the chambers.

mistakes.r: Reduced blood flow means a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
mistakes.w: The heart muscle needs less blood so it stops.

mistakes.r: Rejection happens because the recipient's immune system recognises the foreign antigens and attacks the organ.
mistakes.w: Rejection happens because the donor heart is too small.

mistakes.r: Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive while waiting for a transplant, or to let the heart rest.
mistakes.w: Artificial hearts are a permanent cure.

mistakes.r: Neither is simply better; evaluate using speed, risk, cost and whether it treats the cause.
They last a long time but patients usually need anticoagulants and these cause a bleeding risk.
mistakes.w: Mechanical valves have no disadvantages because they last for ever.

mistakes.r: Statins lower blood cholesterol, which slows the build-up of fatty deposits; they do not remove existing deposits or open the artery quickly.
mistakes.w: Says statins unblock the artery straight away.

summary: You must explain how fatty deposits narrow the coronary arteries and reduce the oxygen reaching the heart muscle, and evaluate four treatments: statins, stents, valve replacement and heart transplants or artificial hearts. It matters because CHD is a leading cause of death and 'evaluate' questions are worth up to 6 marks.

Blood in the chambers does not feed the heart wall. A fatty deposit in a coronary artery narrows the lumen, so less blood reaches the muscle beyond it (shaded orange), which therefore gets less oxygen for aerobic respiration.

svg.cap: Stent procedure, in a longitudinal section of a coronary artery. (1) A thin tube (catheter) carries a folded wire mesh tube (stent) on a balloon to the narrowing. (2) The balloon is inflated, expanding the stent and pressing the fatty deposit against the artery wall. (3) The balloon is deflated and removed. (4) The stent stays in place and holds the artery open so blood can again reach the heart muscle. The effect is immediate, but a stent treats the narrowing, not the cause.

svg.cap: Heart valves in a simplified longitudinal section (flaps = valve leaflets). A healthy valve opens to let blood flow forwards and closes to stop it flowing back. A faulty valve may not open fully (stiff, flow restricted) or may not close properly (leaky, blood flows backwards). Either way the heart pumps less effectively, so the valve can be replaced with a biological valve (from an animal or human donor) or a mechanical valve.

terms.d: A disease in which layers of fatty material build up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
The arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
The central space inside a blood vessel through which blood flows.
A fatty substance in the blood; when levels are high it is deposited in artery walls.
A drug that reduces blood cholesterol levels, slowing down the rate at which fatty material is deposited.
A wire mesh tube put into an artery to keep it open.
A flap of tissue that stops blood flowing backwards in the heart.
A replacement valve taken from a human or an animal.
A replacement valve made from artificial materials.
A drug that reduces blood clotting, taken by patients with mechanical valves.
A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood around the body.
Replacing a failing organ with a healthy one from a donor.
When the recipient's immune system attacks a transplanted organ because it has foreign antigens.
A mechanical pump used to keep a patient alive while waiting for a transplant, or to allow the heart to rest and recover.
A disease that is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be spread from person to person.
Something linked to an increased rate of a disease.
A valve that does not open fully, restricting the flow of blood.
A valve that does not close properly, so blood flows backwards.

worked.ans: Layers of fatty material build up in the coronary arteries and narrow them, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. This means the heart muscle receives less oxygen, so its cells cannot release enough energy by aerobic respiration, causing damage (a heart attack).
worked.q: Explain how coronary heart disease can cause a heart attack. (3 marks)
steps: Fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries, narrowing the lumen.
So less blood flows through to the heart muscle.
So there is a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle, which cannot respire aerobically fast enough, and the muscle can be damaged or die.

worked.ans: 8% (statin) and 14% (placebo); heart attacks were reduced by about 43% (42.9%) compared with the placebo group.
worked.q: In a trial, 1000 patients took a statin and 1000 took a placebo for 5 years. 80 patients in the statin group and 140 in the placebo group had a heart attack. Calculate the percentage in each group and the percentage reduction in heart attacks caused by the statin. (4 marks)
steps: Percentage reduction = 6 / 14 x 100 = 42.857 which rounds to 42.9%.

worked.ans: A stent holds the coronary artery open so blood flow to the heart muscle is restored straight away, which is useful for a severely narrowed artery. However it involves an operation with risk of infection and blood clots and it does not stop fatty material building up elsewhere. Statins reduce blood cholesterol, so they slow the rate at which fatty material is deposited, which treats the cause and needs no surgery, but they act slowly, must be taken for a long time, and can have side effects. Overall, a stent is better for a patient whose artery is badly blocked and needs urgent relief, whereas statins are better for long-term prevention; many patients would benefit from both.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of a stent compared with taking statins for a patient with CHD. (6 marks)
steps: Stent: advantage is quick, immediate restoration of blood flow; disadvantage is surgery risks and clots, and it does not treat the cause.
Statins: advantage is tablets, no surgery, treat the cause by reducing cholesterol; disadvantage is slow, long term, side effects.
Conclusion: match to the patient and justify.
